title: The Pudding That Paid for Free Flights

sources.claim: In 1999 civil engineer David Phillips bought 12,150 cups of Healthy Choice pudding during a frequent-flyer promotion
He spent about $3,140 and received about 1,253,000 miles
Offer: 500 miles per 10 barcodes; early entries earned a bonus
Pudding was donated to the Salvation Army and food banks, whose volunteers removed the labels
Airlines sell miles to promotional partners for about two cents a mile

lines.text: In 1999, an engineer bought twelve thousand cups of chocolate pudding, and he never planned to eat one.

shot.setting: extreme close-up on a conveyor belt
shot.action: one pudding cup slides past, then dozens more pile up

shot.setting: a 1999 American supermarket checkout, fluorescent lights
shot.action: a lanky engineer with glasses pushes a shopping cart overflowing with chocolate pudding cups toward a shocked cashier

lines.text: The cashier thought he was crazy.

shot.action: the cashier stares wide-eyed at the conveyor belt full of pudding cups

lines.text: You see, the pudding company had printed a deal on every package. Send in ten barcodes, get five hundred frequent flyer miles.

shot.action: Clause the raccoon inspector reads the offer on the package, eyes widening

lines.text: But wait, pudding? Why not frozen dinners or soup?

shot.action: the engineer compares a frozen dinner and a soup can, unimpressed

lines.text: He checked. Everything else cost dollars, not cents.
Then, in a discount store, he found the pudding cups. Twenty-five cents each.

shot.noun: pudding cups on a clearance shelf
shot.action: the engineer freezes in front of a shelf of pudding cups under a glowing 25 cent sign

lines.text: So he bought one cart. Then ten carts. Then every cup in every store across town.

shot.action: the engineer pushes one cart, then a train of ten carts

shot.noun: map of town with store pins
shot.action: pudding cup icons pop up on every store on a town map

lines.text: "Sir, are you opening a restaurant?" a manager asked. "Something like that."

shot.action: a suspicious store manager in a red vest questions the engineer next to stacked pudding boxes

lines.text: Now he had twelve thousand puddings and a deadline. Peeling every barcode himself would take forever.

shot.setting: suburban garage packed floor to ceiling with pudding boxes
shot.action: the engineer sits exhausted holding one peeled barcode

lines.text: So he drove the pudding to the Salvation Army. Their volunteers peeled the labels, and they got to keep the pudding.

shot.action: a long table of cheerful volunteers peeling barcodes off pudding cups into a bucket

lines.text: You see, the airlines had already sold those miles to the pudding company for about two cents each, so his barcodes were already paid for.

shot.noun: miles flowing from airline to pudding company
shot.setting: cutaway diagram of an airline office connected by pipes to a pudding factory
close-up of a two-cent price tag on a stack of airline miles certificates

lines.text: And because he mailed them early, a bonus doubled everything.

shot.action: envelopes of barcodes burst out of a mailbox

lines.text: Three thousand dollars of pudding became one point two five million miles.

shot.action: the engineer relaxes in a first-class seat holding a single pudding cup, a jet soaring

lines.text: Send this to your friend who never reads the fine print.

shot.setting: close-up of a pudding package label

lines.text: Legal? Completely. Smart? Clause says: approved.

shot.noun: red APPROVED stamp on case file
shot.action: Clause the raccoon inspector slams a red APPROVED stamp onto a manila folder labeled CASE #001

lines.text: Would you have bought twelve thousand puddings?

shot.action: Clause raises one eyebrow and holds up a pudding cup to the camera

closing.teaser: Case #002: the lifetime plane ticket an airline regretted
